<?php

namespace App\Jobs\Notifications;

use App\Services\Notifications\NotificationPublisher;
use Illuminate\Bus\Queueable;
use Illuminate\Contracts\Queue\ShouldQueue;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Bus\Dispatchable;
use Illuminate\Queue\InteractsWithQueue;
use Illuminate\Queue\SerializesModels;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Log;

// V2: Marks expired affiliate invites and publishes expiry notifications to brand managers.
class InviteExpirySweepJob implements ShouldQueue
{
    use Dispatchable, InteractsWithQueue, Queueable, SerializesModels;

    public int $tries = 1;

    public int $timeout = 120;

    public function __construct()
    {
        $this->onQueue('notifications');
    }

    public function handle(NotificationPublisher $publisher): void
    {
        $now = now();

        $expired = DB::table('brand.brand_affiliate_invites')
            ->where('status', 'pending')
            ->where('expires_at', '<', $now)
            ->get(['id', 'brand_professional_id', 'email', 'first_name']);

        foreach ($expired as $invite) {
            try {
                DB::table('brand.brand_affiliate_invites')
                    ->where('id', $invite->id)
                    ->where('status', 'pending') // guard against concurrent updates
                    ->update(['status' => 'expired', 'updated_at' => $now]);

                $brandId = trim((string) ($invite->brand_professional_id ?? ''));
                if ($brandId === '') {
                    continue;
                }

                $label = trim((string) ($invite->first_name ?? ''));
                if ($label === '') {
                    $label = trim((string) ($invite->email ?? ''));
                }
                if ($label === '') {
                    $label = 'An invitee';
                }

                $publisher->publish(
                    professionalId: $brandId,
                    frontendType: 'Warning',
                    category: 'invites',
                    title: 'Invite expired',
                    body: "Your invite to {$label} has expired.",
                    dedupeKey: "invite.expired.{$invite->id}",
                    ctaUrl: '/account/affiliates',
                    retentionConfigKey: 'invite',
                );
            } catch (\Throwable $e) {
                Log::warning('InviteExpirySweepJob failed for invite', [
                    'invite_id' => $invite->id,
                    'message' => $e->getMessage(),
                ]);
            }
        }
    }

    public function failed(\Throwable $e): void
    {
        Log::error('Invite expiry sweep job failed', [
            'message' => $e->getMessage(),
        ]);
    }
}

2. Bump `$timeout` from 120 to 300
3. Bump `$tries` from 1 to 3

The `chunkById` on a `DB::table()` query builder works, but I need to be careful - `chunkById` on the query builder requires an `id` column. Since we're selecting `['id', 'brand_professional_id', 'email', 'first_name']`, the `id` column is already included.


I'm setting up the chunkById call with the chunk size, closure, and letting it default to the id column for pagination...

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
`chunkById` on the Laravel query builder works similarly to Eloquent's — it paginates using keyset-based cursor logic (`WHERE id > last_seen_id`) rather than `OFFSET`, which means consistent performance even on large tables. The key requirement: the `id` column must be in the select list, which it already is here.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

All decisions are clear — no questions needed. The fix is mechanical: wrap the loop body in `chunkById(500, ...)`, close over `$publisher` and `$now`, and bump the class properties.

input.content:
## Plain English
The daily job that marks expired affiliate invites used to pull every expired invite into memory all at once before processing them. If there were thousands of expired invites, this could cause the job to run out of memory and crash. The fix processes them in batches of 500 at a time, so memory usage stays flat no matter how many invites accumulate. The job also now gets more time and retry attempts before giving up.

## Technical Summary
Changed `InviteExpirySweepJob::handle()` in `app/Jobs/Notifications/InviteExpirySweepJob.php` to replace `DB::table(...)->get()` + `foreach` with `->chunkById(500, closure)`. The closure closes over `$publisher` and `$now` from the outer scope. Per-invite try/catch remains unchanged, preserving fault isolation within each chunk. Class properties bumped: `$timeout` 120 → 300, `$tries` 1 → 3.

## Decisions Made
- Chunk size of 500: reasonable middle ground — small enough to cap memory, large enough to minimize per-chunk query overhead on a table expected to stay in the thousands range.
- Kept `$now` captured at handle() entry rather than re-capturing inside the chunk closure, so all rows in a single sweep share the same expiry timestamp boundary (avoids edge cases where rows just crossing the boundary mid-sweep get inconsistent treatment).

## Notes
`chunkById` on the query builder uses keyset pagination (`WHERE id > ?`) rather than OFFSET, so it stays performant even if the expired-invite set is large. The `id` column was already in the original select list, satisfying `chunkById`'s requirement.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
`chunkById` uses keyset pagination (`WHERE id > last_id LIMIT 500`) rather than SQL `OFFSET`, which means query time stays constant regardless of how far into the dataset you are — unlike offset-based chunking which gets progressively slower. This is why Laravel has both `chunk()` (offset-based) and `chunkById()` (keyset-based), and why `chunkById` is almost always the right choice for large table sweeps.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
